questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman was reviewed on the ward due to nausea and several diarrheal stools. She had recently sustained a cerebrovascular accident. She had no known drug allergies. Investigations: Total white cell count 22,000/mm3 Serum creatinine 2.5 mg/dL Normal liver function tests Blood and urine cultures were positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sensitivities pending
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ceftazidime IV Aztreonam is best reserved for treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in patients with severe beta-lactam allergy. The patient is not a candidate for oral antibiotic therapy due to recent gastrointestinal disturbances. The patient is also elderly, has renal insufficiency, and has experienced recent central nervous system pathology, each of which increases risk for carbapenem-induced seizures. Aminoglycoside therapy would be risky given the patient’s renal function and is not preferred for monotherapy of serious Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections. Ceftazidime is a first-line therapy for treatment of Pseudomonas infections.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q5

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of fevers. She had AML for which she was on induction chemotherapy. She had a tunneled intravenous catheter. On examination, there were no signs of infection around her CVC site. There were two necrotic skin lesions on her right lower leg. Investigations: Neutrophil count 0.1 ×109/L Blood and wound cultures grew gram-negative bacilli
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Pseudomonas infections are commonly considered as important causes of neutropenic fever. This patient presented also with skin lesions, which could be consistent with ecthyma gangrenosum, of which Pseudomonas is an important cause. The other gram-negative bacteria listed can certainly cause BSI but would be less likely in this scenario.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q15

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman was diagnosed with healthcareassociated pneumonia. She was a nursing home resident with no drug allergies, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and acute on chronic kidney disease. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 25 mL/min (baseline creatinine clearance 40 mL/min) Sputum culture negative Multiplex PCR respiratory virus panel negative
questions.lead_in: What antipseudomonal agent poses the greatest risk for neurotoxicity?
questions.explanation: Cefepime While each of the beta-lactam antibiotics listed has the potential to cause neurotoxicity, cefepime is most associated with the development of this adverse effect. A US Food and Drug Administration safety alert for cefepime identified age >50 and inadequate renal dosing adjustments as risk factors for neurotoxicity.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q4

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient admitted with STEMI, now status-post CABG, and with a complicated hospital course thereafter, including prolonged respiratory failure requiring tracheostomy and gastrostomy tube placements, who also received several days of broad-spectrum antibiotics postoperatively because of shock, and concern for possible sepsis, is now having increasing supplemental oxygen requirement and fever. His chest radiograph shows diffuse pulmonary opacities, worst in the right-lower lobe. His nurse also has noted increasingly profuse and purulent tracheal secretions. He was started on linezolid and meropenem, but after 2 days he was still having fevers, and his respiratory status continued to worsen. Tracheal aspirate culture is now growing an organism that was identified as an oxidase-positive, nonfermenting gram-negative bacillus.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia This patient has hospital-acquired pneumonia and did not demonstrate clinical improvement on broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. He has multiple risk factors for development of drug-resistant pathogens, including his prolonged ICU stay and antecedent antibiotic therapy. Linezolid and meropenem would provide more than adequate activity against most gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens, including those that would produce extended-spectrum β-lactamases. Stenotrophomonas can be a cause of HAP , is intrinsically resistant to the antibiotic agents that he has been receiving, and is a nonfermenting gram-negative bacillus that is oxidase-positive. Other nonfermenting, oxidase-positive gram-negative bacilli include Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Achromobacter, and Burkholderia, among others.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q31

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with 4 days of mildly pruritic rash, predominantly around his groin, and on his legs. He was otherwise feeling well. On exam, he was noted to have multiple punctate areas of erythema, surrounding hair follicles in his groin and on both legs. He had no palmoplantar lesions. He also mentioned that he had spent several hours in his hot tub the week before he noticed the rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his folliculitis?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa This patient likely has hot tub folliculitis, which is most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa . This infection is usually self-limited and does not require systemic antibiotic therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q30

questions.stem: A 30-year-old firefighter sustained third-degree burns to his forearms and hands. He was admitted to the burn unit and underwent wound debridement that evening. The next day, he developed significant erythema and induration involving his burn wounds.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus Gram-positive bacteria ( Staphylococcus, Streptococcus) are the most common organisms associated with burn wound infections immediately following injury. The shift to gramnegative bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa , Acinetobacter spp.) and fungi occurs several days later, particularly with prolonged hospitalization and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q28

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man presented with fever and a new skin lesion. He was known to have had a prolonged neutropenia for at least 28 days following chemotherapy. He had a tunnelled line in situ which had been placed 10 days earlier. On examination, his temperature was 38.7°C. He had an erythematous lesion with central necrosis on his left leg. It was nontender.
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa This is a picture typical of ecthyma gangrenosum. Ecthyma gangrenosum is classically associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia in the setting of immunocompromise. It can also (but less commonly) develop with Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Candida albicans among others, especially gram-negatives. It is usually due to hematogenous dissemination of the pathogen, with subsequent invasion of small vessel walls, leading to ischemia and necrosis distally. Typically lesions start as painless macules which evolve rapidly into indurated bullae which then become necrotic. Multiple molds can invade the vascular endothelium causing necrotic skin lesions as well as systemic involvement, such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, and Mucor. In the setting of neutropenia and necrotic skin lesions, additional imaging seeking thoracic and abdominal lesions due to angioinvasive molds would also be appropriate.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q49

questions.question: Name the most likely mechanism of resistance

parts.text: Serratia marcescens resistant to ertapenem, imipenem AND meropenem, but susceptible to Ceftriaxone
Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to Meropenem, but susceptible to Imipenem
Staphylococcus aureus resistant to daptomycin
Enterococcus gallinarum resistant to vancomycin, but susceptible to teicoplanin
Enterobacter cloacae intermediate to ertapenem, but susceptible to meropenem and cefepime

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). Pseudomonas: RND efflux pump MexAB-OprM (meropenem/doripenem, but not imipenem, are substrates of this efflux system). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. Enterobacter cloacae: Hyperexpression of ampC + porin change combination.

parts.text: Ceftolozane-tazobactam in MDR pseudomonas. Name three resistance mechanisms that it can overcome.

cohort_answer.text: Overexpression of efflux pumps; Loss of the outer membrane porin OprD; Not affected by beta lactamases both AmpC and ESBLs; Overcomes modification of PBPs

parts.text: 22. What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

cohort_answer.text: Not affected by ESBL or AmpC enzymes; not affected by active efflux (upregulation of MexXY, MexAB); not appreciably affected by porin channel loss of OprD (cannot overcome MBL; not active against class A KPC, contrary to ceftaz-avi)

questions.question: 60 yo lady with c diff after being on cipro for a month.

parts.text: What are 2 treatment options for her?
Pick which are the lowest risk for C diff : macrolide, pen, ceph, doxy, clinda, fluoroquinolones
She now comes back with a second recurrence. Name 2 abx regimens you would consider and 2 non-abx therapies

questions.model_answer: a) Treatment options for first C. diff episode: (1) Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID x10 days (preferred). (2) Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID x10 days (alternative). b) Lowest risk of C. diff among listed classes: doxycycline (tetracyclines carry the lowest associated risk; fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, and cephalosporins carry highest risk). c) Second recurrence: antibiotic regimens (2): (1) Vancomycin in a tapered/pulsed regimen. (2) Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID x10 days (standard or extended-pulsed dosing). Non-antibiotic therapies (2): (1) Fecal microbiota transplant. (2) Bezlotoxumab (monoclonal antibody against C. difficile toxin B) as adjunct to antibiotics.

questions.question: A woman goes on an antibiotic for an infection, and later develops diarrhea. She is diagnosed with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea – (2019)

parts.text: What are TWO antimicrobial regimens for this condition/first episode?

Three weeks after completing this therapy, she develops recurrent infection and is treated with the same agent. She then develops another recurrence. List TWO antimicrobial and TWO non-antimicrobial therapies for this condition.
Pick the 3 most likely agents from the list: Penicillin, cephalosporin, macrolide, quinolone, clindamycin, tetracycline.

cohort_answer.text: First episode: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days; Fidaxomicin 200mg PO BID x10 days. Recurrence: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10-14 days with taper and pulse dosing (multiple potential regimens); Fidaxomicin 200mg PO BID x10 days; Fecal transplant; Monoclonal antibody therapy (bezlotoxumab). Most likely causative agents: Cephalosporin, quinolone, clindamycin

questions.question: 25. C diff toxigenic strain confirmed in these 4 scenarios, what is the treatment regimen.

parts.text: 8 month old
adult with first episode, non-severe
child with first episode, non-severe
adult with fulminant colitis
child with 2nd recurrence

questions.model_answer: a) 8-month-old: C. difficile is generally not treated/considered pathogenic in infants <1 year (high asymptomatic colonization rates); supportive care, treat only if severe/no other cause found. b) Adult, first episode, non-severe: fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID x10 days (preferred), or vancomycin 125 mg PO QID x10 days. c) Child, first episode, non-severe: vancomycin 10 mg/kg PO QID (max 125 mg/dose) x10 days, or fidaxomicin per weight-based pediatric dosing x10 days. d) Adult, fulminant colitis: vancomycin 500 mg PO/per rectum QID plus IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h; surgical consult for possible colectomy. e) Child, 2nd recurrence: vancomycin tapered/pulsed regimen, consider fecal microbiota transplant if refractory.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA/SHEA 2021 C. difficile guidelines; pediatric IDSA guidance

questions.question: Resistance mechanisms for the following:

parts.text: Pseudomonas R to mero and imi; sensitive to piperacillin and ceftaz (give two)
E coli R to cefoxitin, ampicillin but intermediately susceptible to CTX

questions.model_answer: a) Pseudomonas resistant to meropenem/imipenem but susceptible to piperacillin/ceftazidime, two mechanisms: (1) Loss/downregulation of OprD porin channel (carbapenem-specific entry porin) - selectively reduces carbapenem entry without affecting piperacillin/ceftazidime. (2) Carbapenem-hydrolyzing enzyme with narrow spectrum not affecting piperacillin/ceftazidime is less typical; more consistent second mechanism is efflux pump overexpression (e.g. MexAB-OprM) combined with OprD loss - accept efflux pump upregulation as second mechanism. b) E. coli resistant to cefoxitin/ampicillin, intermediate to ceftriaxone (cefotaxime): plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamase (e.g. CMY-type) - confers resistance to cephamycins (cefoxitin) and penicillins, with reduced susceptibility extending to third-generation cephalosporins.

questions.question: Question related to antibiotic resistance.

parts.text: Pseudomonas R imipenem and meropenem but S to piperacillin and ceftazidime. Name 2 mechanisms of resistance with molecule/gene (as appropriate)
E coli with R to cefoxitin, amp and cefazolin but I to ceftriaxone. Name one mechanism of resistance with molecule/gene (as appropriate)

questions.model_answer: a) Pseudomonas resistant to imipenem/meropenem, susceptible to piperacillin/ceftazidime - 2 mechanisms with molecule/gene: (1) Loss of OprD porin (oprD gene mutation/downregulation) - selective loss of carbapenem entry. (2) Upregulation of MexAB-OprM efflux pump (mexAB-oprM operon) - effluxes multiple agents but not significantly piperacillin/ceftazidime. b) E. coli resistant to cefoxitin, ampicillin, cefazolin, intermediate to ceftriaxone - mechanism: plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamase (e.g. blaCMY gene) conferring cephamycin (cefoxitin) and narrow-spectrum penicillin/cephalosporin resistance with reduced susceptibility to extended-spectrum cephalosporins.

parts.text: Name two mechanisms of Pseudomonas resistance to IMI and MP?

cohort_answer.text: MBL, carbapenemase; KPC, porins, efflux pump. Mutational loss of OprD porin, conferring resistance to imipenem; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM). Upregulation of the MexXY efflux system (a member of the RND family), which exports fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, aminoglycosides, and antipseudomonal β-lactam agents. Overexpression of AmpC chromosomal β-lactamases conferring resistance to multiple β-lactam antibiotics

questions.question: Mechanism of Resistance

parts.text: For the following isolates, name the mechanism of resistance: Enterobacter; Pseudomonas R to Imi/Mero, S to Ceftaz; GNB R to mero but increased zone with mero + EDTA; E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin

cohort_answer.text: Enterobacter - AmpC. Pseudomonas R to Imi/Mero, S to Ceftaz - Porin mediated and efflux pump. GNB R to mero but increased zone with mero+EDTA - Metallo beta lactamase. E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin - cephalothin breakpoints do not reliably predict susceptibilities of cephalexin and other cephalosporins.

questions.question: Information on Ceftolozane/Tazobactam

parts.text: Name 3 mechanisms of resistance possessed by P. aeruginosa that this antibiotic bypasses

cohort_answer.text: Efflux pumps (MexAB-OprD); Porin mutations (OprD); Modification of PBPs (ceftolozane potent inhibitor of PBP1b and 3); overexpression of AmpC (affinity for PBP4 not significant enough to induce AmpC); Class A and C beta-lactamases (tazobactam inhibits). Not effective against MBL, KPC, or OXA-48 carbapenemases

questions.question: Q61 (2016 PM). 43F from Peru with GN sepsis, rapidly expanding perianal rash.

parts.text: A) What is the cause of the peri-anal rash?
B) What are 3 diagnostic tests to confirm the cause of the rash?
C) What are 2 infections that increase likelihood of severe illness?
D) What are 2 non-infectious causes that increase likelihood of severe disease?

cohort_answer.text: A) Larva currens caused by Strongyloidiasis infection. B) Strongyloides serology; Stool O+P (and possibly urine O+P); biopsy of skin lesion for histopathology. C) HTLV-1; HIV (has been reported in AIDS but not to extent expected, not AIDS-defining); any condition requiring steroid therapy associated with hyperinfection. D) Corticosteroid use; severe malnutrition; hematological malignancies; SOT.

parts.text: Name three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would still render the isolate susceptible to ceftolazane/tazobactam.

questions.model_answer: Mechanisms of Pseudomonas resistance that still leave the isolate susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam (3): (1) Loss of OprD porin (carbapenem resistance without affecting ceftolozane entry). (2) Efflux pump overexpression (e.g. MexAB-OprM, MexXY) - ceftolozane is a poor substrate for these pumps. (3) AmpC overproduction/derepression - ceftolozane is stable to AmpC hydrolysis even when overexpressed, unlike other cephalosporins.

questions.question: Give diagnosis in each scenario:

parts.text: AML patient with line and fever and hemorrhagic bullae
Freshwater injury of head
Asplenic patient fever and hypotension after dog bite
1 or 2-more (scenarios not recalled)

questions.model_answer: a) AML patient with central line and fever with hemorrhagic bullae: ecthyma gangrenosum due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia. b) Freshwater injury of the head: Aeromonas hydrophila infection (also consider Naegleria fowleri if exposure via nasal water and meningoencephalitis symptoms). c) Asplenic patient with fever and hypotension after dog bite: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis. d) [additional scenario not recalled - insufficient information to answer].

parts.text: Pseudomonas resistant to mero and imi, susceptible to ceftaz, piptaz. 2 resistance mechanisms.
E. coli resistant to ampicillin, cefazolin, cefoxitin (MIC >256), intermediate to ceftriaxone. Mechanism?

questions.model_answer: a) Pseudomonas resistant to meropenem/imipenem, susceptible to ceftazidime/piperacillin-tazobactam - 2 mechanisms: (1) Loss of OprD porin channel (selective carbapenem entry loss). (2) Efflux pump overexpression (MexAB-OprM/MexXY-OprM). b) E. coli resistant to ampicillin, cefazolin, cefoxitin (MIC >256), intermediate to ceftriaxone - mechanism: plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamase (e.g. CMY-type) production.

questions.question: You are seeing a patient with multi-drug resistant Pseudomonas that is resistant to cefepime, ceftazidime, imipenem, meropenem, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, and colistin.

parts.text: Based on the 2023 IDSA guidelines for resistant gram negatives, name FOUR potential options for treatment of this infection?
Which one of the above agents would work in the presence of a metallo-beta lactamase?

questions.model_answer: a) Four treatment options for pan-resistant Pseudomonas (resistant to cefepime, ceftazidime, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, colistin) per 2023 IDSA resistant gram-negative guidance: (1) Ceftolozane-tazobactam (if susceptible - active against many efflux/AmpC/porin-mediated resistant strains, though not routinely active against carbapenemase producers). (2) Ceftazidime-avibactam. (3) Imipenem-relebactam. (4) Cefiderocol (siderophore cephalosporin with broad activity including MDR/XDR Pseudomonas). b) Agent effective in presence of metallo-beta-lactamase (MBL): cefiderocol (not hydrolyzed/inactivated by MBLs, unlike avibactam- and relebactam-based combinations which do not inhibit MBLs).
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA 2023 guidance on treatment of AMR gram-negative infections

questions.question: Q35 (2016 PM). Antimicrobial Mechanism of Resistance. a) Name 3 mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would still render the isolate susceptible to Ceftolozane/Tazobactam

parts.text: Name 3 mechanisms that would still leave isolate susceptible to Ceftolozane/Tazobactam

cohort_answer.text: Loss of OprD porin channel (typically carbapenem resistance); AmpC hyperproduction (chromosomal beta-lactamases); efflux pump (that pumps out other antibiotics but not ceftolozane/tazobactam); MexXY efflux system (exports fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams); aminoglycoside modifying enzyme; parC/gyrA mutations; OXA-48 beta-lactamases.

questions.question: Q37 (2014). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. What is the mechanism of resistance in the following scenarios: Serratia (Ertapenem R, Imipenem R, Meropenem R, CFTx S); Pseudomonas (Meropenem R, Imipenem S); E. gallinarum (Vancomycin R); E. cloacae (Cefepime S, Meropenem S, Ceftazidime R, Ertapenem R); MRSA (Daptomycin R); MRSA (Linezolid R)

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each scenario

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Serratia marcescens enzyme (SME) - carbapenemase Class A. Pseudomonas: MexAB-OprM efflux cassette. E. gallinarum: VanC gene presence (chromosomal). E. cloacae: intrinsic resistance to inducible AmpC (R to beta-lactams); OXA-48 (R to Erta, S to Mero with additional efflux pump or porin). MRSA Daptomycin R: mprF gene (phosphatidylglycerol lysyltransferase). MRSA Linezolid R: 23S RNA G2576T point mutation.

questions.question: Q43 (2012 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Enterobacter (unspecified); Pseudomonas - Imi/Mero (R), Ceftaz (S); GNB - Mero (R), increased zone with Mero+EDTA; E coli - Cephalothin (R), Cefazolin (S)

parts.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario

cohort_answer.text: Enterobacter - AmpC. Pseudomonas (Imi/Mero R, Ceftaz S) - loss of OprD (porin mutation). GNB (Mero R, increased zone with Mero+EDTA) - metallo-beta-lactamase. E coli (Cephalothin R, Cefazolin S) - beta-lactamase (likely SHV).

questions.question: Q46 (2010 AM, 2009 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance (fill in the blank table): K. pneumoniae with Meropenem; P. aeruginosa with Meropenem; E faecium with penicillin; E faecalis with high level aminoglycoside resistance; S. pneumoniae with moxifloxacin; S. pyogenes with erythromycin

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair

cohort_answer.text: K. pneumoniae/Meropenem: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A KPCs; reduced expression of OmpK35/OmpK36. P. aeruginosa/Meropenem: downregulated/absent OprD porin with background AmpC; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM-1 less common); upregulation of MexA-MexB-OprM efflux (resistant to mero/doripenem but not imipenem). E. faecium/Penicillin: altered PBPs (resistant pbp5 allele). E. faecalis/HLAR: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2'')-Ia. S. pneumoniae/Moxifloxacin: dual mutations in GyrA and ParC. S. pyogenes/Erythromycin: erm gene (ribosome methylation) - methylase enzymes dimethylate adenine on 23S rRNA of 50S subunit, disrupting MLS binding.

questions.question: Q48 (2011 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Pseudomonas mechanisms of resistance.

parts.text: A) Isolate is Resistant to Imi and Mero. What are 2 mechanisms of resistance?
B) The isolate is susceptible to PipTazo and Ceftaz (?)

cohort_answer.text: A) Porin loss (OprD); upregulated efflux pump (MexXY); less commonly acquired carbapenemase. Common P. aeruginosa mechanisms: derepression of AmpC chromosomal beta-lactamases; mutational loss of OprD (Imi>Mero); MexA/MexB (Mero>Imi); upregulation of MexXY efflux system (exports FQ, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams). B) Porin loss OprD; efflux pumps MexXY-OprM.

questions.question: Q49 (2008). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism(s) involved: a) Enterobacter - CTZ (R), CTX (R), PipTazo (R), Imipenem (S); b) E coli - Amp (R), Cefazolin (S), Cephalothin (I); c) Pseudomonas - Imi/Mero (R), PipTazo/CTZ (S); d) Pseudomonas - Imipenem (R) MIC=64, MIC with EDTA in agar=0.5

parts.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario

cohort_answer.text: a) De-repression of chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase (class C) in presence of beta-lactams. b) SHV beta-lactamase (class A). c) OprD porin loss (efflux pump would also likely render resistant to tazo/ceftaz). d) Metallo-beta-lactamase (class B).

questions.question: Q53 (2007). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism for each, as well as suggested treatment: Macrolides (+ explain D test); Beta-lactamases; Pseudomonas and carbapenems

parts.text: State mechanisms and treatments for each category

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides: efflux (mefA gene, lower level resistance MIC<=16); ribosomal methylation (ermB gene, high level MIC>=64). D test checks for inducible clindamycin resistance via inducible erm gene - blunting of zone of inhibition around clindamycin proximal to erythromycin disk (D-shaped zone = positive, indicates induced clindamycin resistance); suggested treatment: beta-lactam or vancomycin for GPC, septra for MRSA. Beta-lactamases: bacteria produce enzymes breaking down beta-lactam (penicillinase, cephalosporinase/ESBL, carbapenemase); treatment depends on spectrum - use cephalosporin/aztreonam/carbapenem, add beta-lactamase inhibitor, or switch classes (tigecycline, colistin). Pseudomonas and carbapenems: porin loss (OprD deficiency confers high resistance esp to imipenem); efflux pump; carbapenemase.

questions.question: Q56 (2004). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. List and describe 3 mechanisms by which P. aeruginosa are resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics. Give an example of an antibiotic affected by each. Also cover Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, MDR

parts.text: Describe resistance mechanisms with examples for beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and MDR

cohort_answer.text: Beta-lactams: Enzymatic inhibition (AmpC cephalosporinases - Ceftazidime; ESBL); Upregulation of efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM - resistance to Meropenem but S to imipenem; MexXY-OprM - resistant to Cefepime but S to Ceftazidime); Decreased outer membrane porin expression (loss of OprD channel - Meropenem, Imipenem). Aminoglycosides: Enzymatic inhibition (AAC6, ANT2); Efflux (MexXY); Ribosomal methylation. Fluoroquinolones: Multidrug efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM, MexCD-OprJ, MexEF-OprN); alteration of target enzymes (DNA gyrase gyrA mutations, topoisomerase parC). MDR: MexAB-OprM and MexXY-OprM efflux systems (RND family) confer intrinsic multidrug resistance to fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, tetracyclines, tigecycline, chloramphenicol.

questions.question:
Q54 (2010 AM)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa

parts.text: A) What are 2 distinct skin manifestations of P. aeruginosa?

cohort_answer.text: Ecthyma gangrenosum; Burn wound infections; Folliculitis associated with hot tub exposures; Foot infection following nail puncture injury; Green nail syndrome (paronychia); Perichondritis following ear piercing or acupuncture; Hot foot syndrome; Toe web folliculitis (speaker notes: Ecthyma gangrenosum, hot tub folliculitis, green toenail)

questions.question: Identify the mechanism: A Pseudomonas isolate is R carbapenems, S PTZ - what is the mechanism of resistance? An E coli isolate is R cefoxitin, S PTZ, S carbapenem, S ceftazidime. What mechanism of resistance?

parts.text: Pseudomonas R carbapenems, S PTZ - mechanism?
E coli R cefoxitin, S PTZ, S carbapenem, S ceftazidime - mechanism?

cohort_answer.text: Pseudomonas: OprD porin mutation (does not cause Piptazo resistance). E. coli: unclear/possibly misremembered stem; discussion suggests possible TEM-1/SHV-1 or AmpC, though the given susceptibility pattern is inconsistent with classic AmpC or ESBL patterns.

questions.question: 22. What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

parts.text: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

cohort_answer.text: Unaffected by porin channels (Mandell); unaffected by upregulation of efflux pumps (Mandell); MexXY efflux system (exports fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam agents); Enzymes: TEM-1, SHV-1, CTX-M, AmpC or ESBL (chromosomal beta lactamases); Aminoglycoside modifying enzymes (reduce susceptibility to all AG).

parts.text: Which bugs are intrinsically resistant to which agents? (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas)

cohort_answer.text:
Pseudo: R- Tigecycline, R- Septra, S-Imipenem
Acinetobacter: S- Septra, S- tige, S- Imi

questions.question: Patient with febrile neutropenia, shown a picture of ecthyma gangrenosum.

parts.text: Two possible diagnoses (one to species level, one to genus level).
Empiric antimicrobial tx pending further investigations?

cohort_answer.text: A) Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staph aureus, Strep pyogenes; fungal: Candida albicans, Mucor, Aspergillus, Fusarium. B) PipTazo (antipseudomonal) or Meropenem; double cover with aminoglycoside if critically ill; add anti-MRSA agent (Vanco) if critically ill.

questions.question: Recreational water exposure

parts.text: 2 causes of infectious dermatitis from hot tub exposure?
1 (or 2) causes of pneumonia from hot tub exposure
Most common parasitic cause of widespread waterborne diarrheal illness?

cohort_answer.text: Dermatitis: Hot tub folliculitis (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) - painful pruritic pustules within 24-48h, self-resolves 7-14d; Hot foot syndrome (Pseudomonas) - painful red nodular lesions on soles, self-limiting 7-10d; Green nail syndrome (pseudomonas) with onychomycosis; Mycobacterium species. Pneumonia: MAC hypersensitivity pneumonitis ('hot tub lung'), usually self-limiting, may need prednisone +/- antimycobacterial; Legionellosis (usually L. pneumophila). Parasite: Giardia lamblia (most common cause of parasitic diarrhea worldwide; cryptosporidium also very high incidence); tx metronidazole/tinidazole/nitazoxanide, paromomycin if pregnant first trimester
